answer.exemplar: The conclusion is drawing a general property out of one specific control. Transport encryption protects the path between two endpoints, and the certificate checks are what establish that the endpoint at the other end is the one that was asked for, so what the combination buys is that a party observing the route cannot read what crosses it or alter it unnoticed. That is the whole of the claim, and it is a substantial claim. Three things sit outside it and each of them is where teams actually lose data. The application is untouched by it: a service that builds a query out of a value from a request, or writes a value from a request into the page it returns, is just as reachable through a protected connection as through an open one, and protecting the route changes nothing about the code that mishandles the value once it arrives. The endpoint is untouched by it in the sense that matters, because anything that reaches the server reads the data after it has been decrypted, so a copy of the file on disk is as readable as it ever was and at-rest controls still apply unchanged. And the route itself only hides content, not shape, since a party on it can still see which two addresses are exchanging data and how much, which is why a protected connection is not a privacy control. The correct response to the team's conclusion is not to turn the transport off; it is to stop treating it as evidence about anything except the route, and to spend the review effort on the code that runs after the decryption finishes.

questions.explanation: The reasoning error in the conclusion is a scope error: a control that protects a segment is being read as evidence about the whole system. Its protection ends at each endpoint, and both the code that processes the request and the data written afterwards are on the far side of that line, so nothing about them is changed by the protection being present. Treating it as a privacy control is a second, separate mistake, since the route can see which addresses are talking and how much data moves, which is metadata the encryption does not touch. The corrective action is to keep the transport protection and move the review effort to the code and the storage behind it, rather than to treat the green padlock as a finding.

questions.explanation: The balance was read once, the two conditions were decided from that read, and the writes happen afterwards, so anything that changed the balance or the status in between leaves the decision describing a state that no longer exists. The shape is the same as the one demonstrated with a file that is found and then removed before it is opened: the check said yes and the action found something other than yes. Ordinary concurrency is enough to produce this, so it does not need a party arranging it, and the second option is the belief that a sequence of statements in one process is a single indivisible step, which is true of one request and false of two requests running at once. The repair is to make the condition and the action one indivisible operation, so that the decision and the change cannot be separated.

questions.stem: A service accepts a byte string from a caller and turns it back into live objects using a mechanism that can create any of a large set of types. What is the risk?
questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Rebuilding objects out of untrusted bytes

answer.exemplar: A trust boundary is where a value the party does not control starts choosing what the system does, and this step is that point, for a reason that has nothing to do with how carefully the bytes are checked. A reader converts text into a value, and the set of things a reader can produce is decided by the format rather than by the text: a field can hold a number or a string, and the parser will produce a number or a string and nothing else. A reconstruction step is different because the bytes carry a name, the mechanism looks that name up, and it constructs whatever it finds, and for most types constructing involves running that type's own initialisation logic, which may read a value, open something, or make a call. So the input is not data that will be validated, it is a specification of what to build, and the number of decisions available to it is the number of types the mechanism knows. That is also why a size limit or a shape check does not help, since both of them are still statements about the description rather than about the effect, and a perfectly well-formed description can name something with a costly constructor. The durable answer is to remove the construction step rather than to harden it: accept a plain data format in which every value is a number, a string, a list or a map, and rebuild the application's own objects from those values in code that the input cannot influence, so the input describes data and never selects behaviour. Where an existing format cannot be replaced, the narrowing measures are a type allowlist, disabling the mechanism on paths reachable from outside, and treating the reconstruction step as the single place where the boundary is crossed rather than spreading partial checks across the code that consumes the result.

questions.explanation: The boundary is crossed at this step because the input stops being a value and becomes a specification of what to build, and the range of effects the input can select is the range of types the mechanism knows rather than the range of shapes the format allows. That is why checks aimed at the shape of the input are beside the point, and why the durable repair is structural: use a format in which the input can only ever describe data, and construct the application's objects in code the input cannot reach. The narrowing measures are worth having where replacement is not possible, but they are reductions in the set of things that can be selected rather than a removal of the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask whether the bytes are a value or a specification, and how many outcomes the mechanism allows.

questions.stem: A hardening review closes every item on its list except four. Which omission leaves the most risk in place, and how is that decided?
questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The line left off the list

answer.exemplar: The recurrence is the clue, and it points at the class of item rather than at the machine. Some hardening items are properties of a machine: a directory permission, an installed component, a service that either runs or does not. Those can be set once and stay set, because nothing in normal operation moves them. Other items are properties of a declaration, and they are only true at the moment something is built or deployed: which permissions the build grants, which addresses the deployment is allowed to reach, which of the product's own services are exposed on which interfaces. A finding of that second kind will reappear on every machine built or deployed from the same declaration, which is exactly what recurring across different machines means, and it will keep reappearing until the declaration changes rather than the machine. So the right diagnosis is that the team has been repairing instances of a defect whose source is upstream, and each repair costs a little effort and buys a little time. Ending the cycle takes two things and only the first is usually attempted. Write the intended settings down as a versioned, checked-in definition, so there is one place that says what the machine should be like and every machine is an instance of it. And then make the deployment compare what it produced against that definition and fail when they differ, so the check runs on every build instead of depending on somebody remembering to look. Once both are in place the finding cannot recur silently, because the build that would produce it no longer completes. The same reasoning applies to the other recurring class, the dependency, where the fix is an equally explicit statement of what may be included and a check that the statement still holds.

questions.explanation: The recurrence identifies the class of item: it is a property of a declaration that is applied at build or deploy time rather than a property of one machine, so repairing machines leaves the source intact and the next build reproduces the same condition. That is why the pattern across different machines is the evidence, and why a fix applied to one instance cannot hold. The cycle ends when the intended state is written down somewhere versioned and a check runs on every build to confirm the machine matches it, which moves the control from a review that depends on somebody remembering into one that the process itself enforces.
questions.hint: Ask whether the item is a property of a machine or of the thing that builds it.
